text: Lesson 14 left you with an approved Phase 1 scope in writing: a unified IT Service Desk for Meridian Health Network's three hospital systems, built inside the Domain Separation structure Technical Architecture already decided. This lesson turns that scope into real catalog items, categories, and flows. Nothing here is invented fresh -- every piece has to trace back to a line in that approved scope, and nothing outside it gets built early just because it would be convenient.

Four pieces make up this build. A catalog item carries the shared top-category list -- Hardware, Software, Access, Facilities-Adjacent, Other -- fixed corporately, with a subcategory field underneath that filters to each caller's own domain, so St. Catherine's keeps its detail and Lakeshore keeps its own list. One Flow Designer flow, not three near-copies, triggers on every request and reads the caller's domain to resolve the correct assignment group. Access-category requests branch into a reusable approval subflow instead of being rebuilt per hospital system.

The routing logic lives in a small Script Include called from the flow's Script step. It looks up the caller's own sys_domain, then checks a mapping table for the assignment group that owns Service Desk work in that specific domain. If no mapping exists for that domain, it falls back to a documented corporate default property instead of guessing -- an explicit, logged fallback, never a silent misassignment that nobody notices until a ticket sits unworked.

The approval subflow carries its own domain check, separate from routing. Before handing an Access request to the built-in Approval action, it resolves the requester's manager and confirms that manager sits in the same domain as the requester. If that check ever fails, the function returns null and logs an error instead of guessing at an approver -- failing closed, so an approval can never accidentally cross a domain boundary it was never supposed to cross.

The service workflows are built, domain-aware from routing through approval. But none of this works yet without real worker data behind it -- a routing script can't look up a caller's domain if that caller's record was never synced into ServiceNow in the first place. Lesson 16 builds exactly that: the platform integration that keeps one hospital system's worker records current.
